source: Alnegheimish et al. (2024) Large language models can be zero-shot anomaly detectors for time series?
finding: SigLLM turns a signal into text and asks an LLM to find anomalies in two ways: PROMPTER (ask directly) and DETECTOR (forecast, then use the residual). DETECTOR clearly beats PROMPTER, which gives many false positives.
numbers: DETECTOR improves F1 by 135% over PROMPTER. Across 11 datasets: LLM F1 is 14.6% above a moving-average baseline and 10.9% below ARIMA. DETECTOR beats Anomaly Transformer on 7 of 11 datasets. Best deep model AER is about 30% better than DETECTOR. LLMs hold the top score on no dataset.
limits: Univariate benchmark signals (NASA SMAP/MSL, NAB, Yahoo), not plant process data. Only GPT-3.5 and Mistral-7B tested.
agent_relevance: A plain LLM is a weaker detector than a classical statistic. Use it for explanation, not as the first-line alarm. Forecast-then-residual beats asking the model to point at anomalies.

source: Alnegheimish et al. (2024) Large language models can be zero-shot anomaly detectors for time series?
finding: Prompting was fragile. GPT and Mistral failed to return clean output unless a chat template was used. Under 'find indices' GPT gave indices past the sequence length. GPT raised a 'repetitive prompt' error on flat windows.
numbers: 23 SMAP signals and 13 MSL signals hit the repetitive-prompt error. Experiments ran over three months of prompt iteration. Runs took hours per dataset and the paper calls the cost high.
limits: Model-specific and dated (2023-24 models).
agent_relevance: Flat, constant sensor stretches (common in plants) break the LLM path. Any agent loop needs a statistical front end and output validation.

source: Zhou and Yu (2025) Can LLMs understand time series anomalies? (ICLR 2025)
finding: Tested seven hypotheses about LLM time-series anomaly detection with synthetic data and affinity-F1. LLMs read series better as images than as text. Chain-of-thought did not help. Repetition bias and arithmetic skill do not explain the ability. Behaviour differs a lot between models.
numbers: Models include GPT-4o-mini, Gemini-1.5-Flash and open Qwen and LLaMA models. Visual input beat text across models and anomaly types; the one exception was frequency anomalies with proprietary models. Authors state they have no evidence LLMs see subtle real-world anomalies.
limits: Mostly synthetic series with trivial anomaly types; few real plant faults.
agent_relevance: Do not add a reasoning step and expect better detection. Render the signal as a plot for a multimodal model. Treat 'understands anomalies' claims as unproven beyond obvious shapes.
quote: LLMs understand time series better as images rather than as text

source: Gruver et al. (2023) Large language models are zero-shot time series forecasters (LLMTime)
finding: Encoding numbers as digit strings lets GPT-3 and LLaMA-2 forecast zero-shot at a level matching or beating trained time-series models. This forecasting is the base of the DETECTOR residual method. GPT-4 did worse than GPT-3.
numbers: Gain depends on tokenisation (spaces force one token per digit for GPT-3; LLaMA-2 differs). Authors blame GPT-4's number tokenisation and poor uncertainty calibration, likely from RLHF.
limits: Forecasting, not fault detection; benchmark series are smooth and seasonal.
agent_relevance: Residual-based fault detection with an LLM needs a forecaster you can trust. Newer alignment can reduce calibration, so test each model.

source: Kim et al. (2022) Towards a rigorous evaluation of time-series anomaly detection (AAAI)
finding: Most published detectors report F1 after 'point adjustment', which credits a whole anomaly segment if one point is hit. This inflates scores so far that random scores beat published methods. An untrained model scores about as well as trained ones without it.
numbers: Point-adjusted F1 vs plain F1 on SWaT and WADI: rank correlation 0.07 and 0.43, Pearson -0.59 and 0.41. Random-score baseline exceeded several published models. Datasets include SWaT and WADI (water plants), SMAP, MSL.
limits: Public datasets only; some labels are known to be noisy.
agent_relevance: Any LLM detection result scored with point adjustment is not comparable. Our agent's checks should compare against a random or untrained baseline.

source: Kim (2026) When LLMs sit above diagnostic tools: unrealized complementarity in industrial fault diagnosis
finding: On five datasets (bearing vibration, process monitoring, semiconductor) an LLM that merges its own judgment with a specialist's output does worse than the specialist alone. Conflicting advice overturned correct LLM answers in all five.
numbers: Tennessee Eastman held-out set: unaided LLM 64.67%, LLM plus specialist 77.43%, specialist alone 83.33%, oracle selector 92.76%. Specialist raised LLM by 12.8 points (95% CI 9.7 to 15.9) but integrated stayed 5.9 points below (CI -12.0 to -0.7). Seven models.
limits: Single author; labels come from a simulator; specialists are simple (logistic regression, random forest).
agent_relevance: Never let the LLM be the last judge over a strong statistical detector. Compare the combined output with the stronger part alone.
quote: an LLM integration layer should be compared with its stronger standalone component, not only with the unaided LLM

source: Kim (2026) When LLMs sit above diagnostic tools
finding: The main integration failure is missed corrections, not harmful acceptance. The model often ignores a correct specialist.
numbers: Missed 140 of 295 correction chances (47.5%). Lost 15 of 99 correct LLM judgments (15.2%); 14 of the 15 copied the specialist's wrong label. Across models the advised call adopted the wrong label 16.4 points more often than a paired repeat call (CI 9.5 to 22.6).
limits: TEP only for this breakdown.
agent_relevance: Add an explicit check that asks whether the specialist's answer should change the verdict, because the default is to under-use good evidence.

source: Kim (2026) When LLMs sit above diagnostic tools
finding: Prompt fixes did not close the gap. An explicit arbitration instruction, giving the stored unaided diagnosis, and swapping to a random-forest specialist all kept the deficit.
numbers: Explicit arbitration minus implicit: -1.3 points (CI -3.1 to +0.5); one table row shows 0 of 99 harmful acceptances but 215 of 295 missed corrections. Stored prior label: 72.2% integrated, -11.1 vs specialist. Random forest specialist 84.0% vs integrated 78.2% (-5.7). Higher reasoning effort raised unaided accuracy 5.2 points (CI 2.2 to 8.2) but did not clearly fix integration.
limits: Secondary analyses, not independent confirmations (author's words).
agent_relevance: Telling the model to arbitrate trades one error type for another. Do not rely on prompt wording alone for source choice.

source: Khan et al. (2024) FaultExplainer: LLMs for interpretable fault detection and diagnosis
finding: Pairs PCA with T2 statistics for detection and top-contributing variables with GPT-4o and o1-preview for root-cause explanation on the Tennessee Eastman Process. Statistics detect; the LLM explains.
numbers: With 15 root causes listed: of 11 PCA-detectable faults GPT-4o got 7, o1-preview 9. Faults 5 and 10 failed for both. With no list (general reasoning) both got 8 of 11 correct or related; both failed Faults 10 and 13. 4 of 15 faults were not detectable by PCA at all.
limits: 11 faults, one run each, no statistics; hallucinated mechanisms reported; limited by which variables PCA selects.
agent_relevance: The statistical stage caps what the LLM can do: if the detector misses a fault the LLM never sees it. Stronger reasoning helped, but list-free diagnosis was no better than a short list.

source: Khan et al. (2024) FaultExplainer
finding: A design that grounds the LLM: give it the PCA contributing variables with percent changes and process descriptions, and optionally past root causes. Failure cases show the LLM explaining deviations by alternative plausible causes instead of the true one.
numbers: Detector set to a 1% false-alarm rate with PCA keeping 90% of variance; example explanations cite specific changes such as A and C feed down 8.90%. Faults 5 and 10 were explained wrongly by both models even with the root-cause list.
limits: Qualitative evaluation by the authors.
agent_relevance: Keep the statistic and its numbers in the prompt; check that the explanation accounts for all top deviating variables.

source: Zhou et al. (2026) Chain of Physics: engineering-inspired LLM reasoning for fault diagnosis
finding: A knowledge graph of failure mode, physical quantity change and sensor, built from asset documents, retrieved as examples, then per-failure-mode LLM calls and a judge. Beats direct prompting and plain RAG on FailureSensorIQ.
numbers: 1,314 single-answer questions. Accuracy direct / RAG / CoP: Claude Opus 4.7 51.98 / 50.61 / 68.80; Llama 3.1 8B 30.75 / 26.86 / 38.51; Qwen 2.5 7B 30.52 / 35.24 / 50.15. Gains 7.8 to 19.6 points over direct, 11.7 to 18.2 over RAG.
limits: Text knowledge questions, not sensor signals. Plain RAG was below direct for two of three models.
agent_relevance: Structured cause-to-observation chains help more than dumping documents into context. Candidate-by-candidate analysis is a usable operator.

source: Zhou et al. (2026) Chain of Physics
finding: Ablation of the staged procedure: most of the gain comes from graph retrieval itself; clarification and the staged judge add small amounts and sometimes hurt.
numbers: Graph retrieval plus one answer call: 66.36 (Opus), 35.16 (Llama), 43.53 (Qwen). Clarification adds 1.45, 1.45, 5.02 points. Full staged pipeline adds a further 0.99, 1.90, 1.60. For Llama 3.1 8B, clarification lowered one split (34.52% before).
limits: Single benchmark; three models.
agent_relevance: Extra reasoning stages give small returns once evidence is structured well; spend effort on the evidence format.

source: Zhou et al. (2026) Chain of Physics
finding: The paper quotes the benchmark's expert baseline: human experts averaged about 60% on FailureSensorIQ and the best expert reached 66.19%. The Opus CoP result of 68.80% is above the best expert.
numbers: Expert mean about 60%, best 66.19%; CoP 68.80% with Claude Opus 4.7.
limits: Benchmark is multiple-choice on documented failure-sensor links; not field diagnosis.
agent_relevance: Knowledge-recall faults are near human level. Open-ended signal diagnosis is where models still lag.

source: McCabe et al. (2026) Can LLM agents efficiently identify appliance faults? (CoffeeBench)
finding: An agent reads 8 simulated sensors, takes actions and guesses a fault among 9 failure modes. Most models fail to identify faults from sensor data alone; the best ones narrow the option space step by step.
numbers: 12 models from four providers. Only one passes 60% accuracy. Three models do about as badly as or worse than a guess-with-elimination baseline (expected 5 turns). Open-weight models time out about ten times more.
limits: Simulated coffee machine, small fault set.
agent_relevance: Elimination (narrowing hypotheses) is what good agents do; weak agents lose track of state.

source: McCabe et al. (2026) CoffeeBench
finding: A 'state tracker' continuation prompt that restates which actions and guesses are done cut timeouts in open-weight models. Initial diagnostic uncertainty and an LLM judge's rating of explanation soundness predict success.
numbers: Agents take over 97% longer when initial uncertainty is high. Soundness of explanations is over 24% higher on successful turns. A soundness-deliberation loop with an LLM judge significantly improved first-guess accuracy in 2 of 3 open-weight models.
limits: One simulator; judge is itself an LLM.
agent_relevance: Useful design: keep an explicit ledger of tests done and hypotheses ruled out; gate the final answer on a soundness check; abstain on high initial uncertainty.

source: Lee et al. (2025) Exploring LLM-based frameworks for fault diagnosis (Hitachi)
finding: On HVAC sensor data LLMs detect faults with high recall but poor precision. Summary statistics as input beat raw series. Several LLMs with specialised prompts beat one LLM for multi-fault labelling. Continual learning from feedback failed.
numbers: Detection: GPT-4o F1 0.84 with accuracy 0.73; a rule-based baseline reached 0.71 accuracy by always saying no fault (F1 zero). Multi-fault classification: GPT-4o F1 about 0.59 with multi-LLM vs at most 0.58 single; GPT-4.1-nano about 0.43. Accuracy fell and stayed low across repeated fault cycles; one raw-data GPT-4o setup recovered.
limits: Simulated HVAC with three fault types; two models; narrow window sizes (24, 36, 48).
agent_relevance: Give the model statistics, not raw numbers. Report F1 not accuracy on imbalanced fault data. Do not assume the model learns from repeated feedback.

source: Wu (2025) A trustworthy industrial fault diagnosis architecture with probabilistic models and LLMs (HCAA)
finding: A Bayesian and rule engine gives the first diagnosis; an LLM arbiter with spectrum charts decides only on conflict; temperature scaling calibrates confidence. Claims large accuracy gains.
numbers: 2,100 vibration samples, 6 fault types plus healthy, 7:2:1 split. Accuracy: naive Bayes 67.1, SVM 68.4, 1D-CNN 79.3, HCAA 95.7 (SD 0.8). ECE 0.188 uncalibrated, 0.041 calibrated.
limits: Single author, small dataset, weak baselines. Opposite in direction to Kim (2026), where the LLM layer hurt. Treat as unreplicated.
agent_relevance: The arbiter-only-on-conflict design is a candidate, but test it against its strongest standalone component.

source: Boonmee et al. (2024) Consultation on industrial machine faults with LLMs
finding: Multi-round prompting claims 91% accuracy on machine fault types over ChatGPT, Claude 2 and CoT baselines.
numbers: The paper reports 85% overall in one table (CoT 80%) and 91% average in another (CoT 77%). The dataset size is left as '[insert number] instances'.
limits: Internal inconsistency and an unfilled placeholder; no real data description. Low reliability.
agent_relevance: Example of a weak source to exclude. Check that headline numbers match the tables.

source: Li and Zhao (2026) S2S-FDD: signals to semantics for zero-shot fault diagnosis
finding: Converts sensor trends into text summaries, then a multi-turn tree-structured diagnosis queries more signals and maintenance documents. Reasoning models do far better than non-reasoning ones here.
numbers: Multiphase flow facility, six fault types, 500 normal samples. DeepSeek-R1 76.92%; QwQ-32B and R1-distill-7B 61.54%; R1-distill-32B 53.85%; Qwen2.5-7B 23.08%; Qwen2.5-72B 30.77%; DeepSeek-V3 23.08%. About 13 test items per model by the table layout.
limits: Very small test, single plant, no statistics; accuracy steps are 7.7 points each.
agent_relevance: Text-summarising signals and tool-calling for extra signals is workable. Reasoning-trained models gain most; parameter count alone did not help.

source: Gopaluni et al. (2026) LLMs in process systems engineering: survey
finding: Fault detection and diagnosis is judged LLMs' clearest process-industry fit because it is language-rich, but real-time, constraint and safety-guaranteed roles stay hard.
numbers: LLM inference 500 to 5000 ms vs PID microseconds to sub-ms and MPC 10 to 100 ms. Most demos use public benchmarks like Tennessee Eastman; few have industrial validation. Cites a knowledge-graph LLM at 98.5% accuracy (Liu 2024a) in aeronautical assembly.
limits: Narrative survey; its claims about other papers were not re-checked here.
agent_relevance: Place the LLM in an advisory layer above conventional detection, with a human and simulation check.

source: Gopaluni et al. (2026) LLMs in process systems engineering: survey
finding: The survey describes an operator workflow: retrieve trends from the historian, query alarm logs, search maintenance records for similar past events, propose a cause, and verify an action in a digital twin before approval. Hallucination of tags, limits and mechanisms is flagged as dangerous.
numbers: Example: temperature up 15 C in 20 minutes, cooling flow down 12%, matched to a past valve incident. Illustrative, no measured results.
limits: Hypothetical scenario, not data.
agent_relevance: A precedent-retrieval plus simulation-check loop fits our schema's test-before-commit idea.

source: Isermann (2006) Fault-diagnosis systems (model-based and signal-based fault detection)
finding: Background anchor for the subfield: detection by limit and trend checks, signal models, parameter estimation and residuals from process models, then symptom-to-fault diagnosis. Statistical detection means checking a residual or a feature against a threshold set from normal data.
numbers: Not opened this session; no numbers recorded.
limits: Book not read; description is from general knowledge and from how the opened papers use residuals and thresholds.
agent_relevance: Maps to our schema: residual = expectation minus observation; detect then isolate. Same pattern as SigLLM DETECTOR.

source: Downs and Vogel (1993) A plant-wide industrial process control problem (Tennessee Eastman)
finding: The Tennessee Eastman Process is the standard simulated chemical plant used by the TEP fault-detection and LLM studies above, with 21 programmed faults. Some faults are known to be hard for PCA.
numbers: Not opened. In FaultExplainer 4 of 15 faults were PCA-undetectable.
limits: Description of the benchmark is from knowledge plus the opened LLM papers.
agent_relevance: TEP is a simulator; results may not transfer to a real plant (the survey says the same).

source: Alnegheimish et al. (2024) SigLLM; Zhou and Yu (2025) read together
finding: Taken together, the two time-series LLM studies agree that LLMs only match simple statistics on easy cases and lag deep detectors. Both found model-to-model variation large.
numbers: SigLLM: deep model AER about 30% better than best LLM path. Zhou and Yu: no evidence beyond trivial anomalies.
limits: Different data and metrics (F1 vs affinity-F1). Not a formal meta-analysis.
agent_relevance: Plan the agent so a statistic does the detecting and the LLM does hypothesis work.

source: Lee et al. (2025) and Kim et al. (2022) read together
finding: Evaluation hygiene matters. Point-adjusted F1 inflates scores; LLM studies use varied metrics (F1, affinity-F1, accuracy). Accuracy is also misleading on imbalanced fault data, as the Hitachi rule-based baseline shows.
numbers: Rule baseline accuracy 0.71 with zero F1 (Lee 2025); random scores beat methods under PA (Kim 2022).
limits: Cross-paper inference by the reviewer.
agent_relevance: When reading or reporting results for the agent, state the metric and the trivial baseline.
